articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: The ECI offers relief to a section of deleted electors but SIR’s flaws remain

Following the Special Summary Revision (SSR) by the Election Commission of India (ECI) in some States that had undergone the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) , mostly in Phases 1 and 2, some 74 lakh names were added onto the electoral rolls. This meant that the electorate in those 13 States, that had shrunk from 49.61 crore to 45.22 crore after the SIR, has now gone up to 45.96 crore. The ECI has extended the SSR to States and UTs in Phase 3. As before, it requires no proof of citizenship or mapping to older rolls, and insists on personal notice before any deletion other than of the dead. It also directs Electoral Registration Officers (EROs) to cross-verify deletions personally wherever they exceed 2% of a polling station’s electors. Draft deletions in Phase 3 of the SIR averaged 17% , and reached 32.8% in Delhi . The ECI also offered another opportunity to electors deleted by the SIR in the seven States and UTs where it is still underway, such as Delhi and Maharashtra, to return to the rolls. Electors who did not return their forms can do so now, explaining the delay, and those who moved within the State can return through the enumeration form with proof of their new address. EROs will process these forms under Rule 21(1) of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, and restore the elector’s old EPIC number.

These “corrective” measures follow the Supreme Court’s observation on October 28 that forcing deleted electors to re-enrol through Form 6, meant for new voters, was an “error”. The ECI’s use of remedies that existed in the registration rules is a tacit admission that it went wrong during the SIR. But the measures are limited. They reach roughly 4.5 crore of the 13.37 crore struck off the draft rolls and do not cover electors who moved out of their States. Electors in States where the SIR has concluded, including Bihar and West Bengal, which have already voted on the SIR rolls, can return only through the SSR, by filing Form 6 as new voters, with fresh EPIC numbers and no record that they were ever on the roll. In essence, the structure of the SIR remains intact. Electors must still provide details from “the last SIR”, and those whose details are unavailable or do not match will be asked for documents in a manner that amounts to a citizenship test. The legality of the ludicrous “logical discrepancy” checks remains unaddressed. The 2002-03 special revision offered a better way. Those who had shifted homes were enumerated door to door at their new addresses. The Supreme Court must direct the ECI to return to that model.

articles.title: Testing times: On India’s two-Test series against New Zealand
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: India needs to be at its best in Tests against New Zealand

New Zealand at home remains an indomitable cricketing opposition. Even the great West Indian squad led by Clive Lloyd suffered a 0-1 Test series defeat in 1980. Pitches that look lush as English meadows, the wind that is often bone-chilling cold, and fast bowlers relishing their prospects, make any tour of New Zealand a difficult outing. So far, the visiting Indians have done well, having won the T20I and ODI series, but the real contest starts with the first Test at Wellington’s Basin Reserve from Thursday. The Shubman Gill-led men’s last overseas tour of Sri Lanka ended with a middling 1-0 victory in the two Tests, but more needs to be done against New Zealand in the latest two-Test series. Placed fourth in the ICC World Test Championship (WTC) table, and with hopes of securing a final berth seemingly fragile, India is in a win-all-games situation first up against New Zealand and later when Australia arrives next year. Against current WTC topper New Zealand, the Indian batters have to stay anchored. This is a line-up that no longer has Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli, Cheteshwar Pujara and Ajinkya Rahane. Gill and company get another opportunity to reiterate their credentials.

For some rugged inspiration they need not look beyond coach Gautam Gambhir in their dressing room. The doughty former India opener batted for 643 minutes while scoring a match-saving 137 in the Napier Test during the 2009 tour. The southpaw will be hoping that the current batting unit, which is high on flair, will remain sober and effectively counter the host. K.L. Rahul, Yashasvi Jaiswal, Devdutt Padikkal and Gill have the onerous task of negating the New Zealand seamers in their backyard. Rishabh Pant and Dhruv Jurel add depth, and if the former can successfully unleash his maverick batting approach, India can upset the host’s best-laid plans. New Zealand will miss the retired Kane Williamson but its batters would be comfortable on familiar surfaces. For India, much would hinge on how Jasprit Bumrah bowls. If the spearhead clicks, then it becomes easier for much of his support-cast that includes the persevering Mohammed Siraj, who was a touch rusty in Sri Lanka. From the squads of the past to the present unit, Ravindra Jadeja remains the link. Whether he will get a role to play or whether the management prefers an all-pace attack, remains a matter of conjecture. The home team led by Tom Latham will depend on Matt Henry, Kyle Jameson and other pacers, to choke the Indian batters. A hard task awaits India, first at Wellington and then at Christchurch.

articles.summary: India needs to be at its best in Tests against New Zealand
articles.keyPoints:
• India needs to be at its best in Tests against New Zealand
• New Zealand at home remains an indomitable cricketing opposition. Even the great West Indian squad led by Clive Lloyd suffered a 0-1 Test series defeat in 1980. Pitches that look lush as English meadows, the wind that is often bone-chilling cold, and fast bowlers relishing their prospects, make any tour of New Zealand a difficult outing. So far, the visiting Indians have done well, having won the T20I and ODI series, but the real contest starts with the first Test at Wellington’s Basin Reserve from Thursday. The Shubman Gill-led men’s last overseas tour of Sri Lanka ended with a middling 1-0 victory in the two Tests, but more needs to be done against New Zealand in the latest two-Test series. Placed fourth in the ICC World Test Championship (WTC) table, and with hopes of securing a final berth seemingly fragile, India is in a win-all-games situation first up against New Zealand and later when Australia arrives next year. Against current WTC topper New Zealand, the Indian batters have to stay anchored. This is a line-up that no longer has Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli, Cheteshwar Pujara and Ajinkya Rahane. Gill and company get another opportunity to reiterate their credentials.
• For some rugged inspiration they need not look beyond coach Gautam Gambhir in their dressing room. The doughty former India opener batted for 643 minutes while scoring a match-saving 137 in the Napier Test during the 2009 tour. The southpaw will be hoping that the current batting unit, which is high on flair, will remain sober and effectively counter the host. K.L. Rahul, Yashasvi Jaiswal, Devdutt Padikkal and Gill have the onerous task of negating the New Zealand seamers in their backyard. Rishabh Pant and Dhruv Jurel add depth, and if the former can successfully unleash his maverick batting approach, India can upset the host’s best-laid plans. New Zealand will miss the retired Kane Williamson but its batters would be comfortable on familiar surfaces. For India, much would hinge on how Jasprit Bumrah bowls. If the spearhead clicks, then it becomes easier for much of his support-cast that includes the persevering Mohammed Siraj, who was a touch rusty in Sri Lanka. From the squads of the past to the present unit, Ravindra Jadeja remains the link. Whether he will get a role to play or whether the management prefers an all-pace attack, remains a matter of conjecture. The home team led by Tom Latham will depend on Matt Henry, Kyle Jameson and other pacers, to choke the Indian batters. A hard task awaits India, first at Wellington and then at Christchurch.

articles.title: Elusive peace: On Kashmir terror attack
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Restoration of Statehood is essential for peace in Jammu and Kashmir

Three months of lull established by security forces in Jammu and Kashmir was rattled by the back-to-back incidents of violence in the past six days. On November 11, a terror attack on a checkpoint manned by the personnel of the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) in Kulgam left three jawans injured. On November 16, a local, whom the police suspected of having joined the terror ranks a few days ago, was killed after six days of a siege-like anti-terror operation in residential areas of Kulgam. In Jammu’s Kishtwar, two Special Police Officers (SPOs) of the J&K Police were found dead with bullet wounds, a day after they were reported missing in a forest range on November 11. The police and the Army, however, remain tight-lipped about the circumstances around the killing of these SPOs, and there are conflicting reports on the circumstances that led to their deaths. The anti-terror operation in civilian areas of Kulgam has raised concerns. Former J&K Chief Minister and PDP president Mehbooba Mufti described the operation, spread over six days, as “collective punishment that only breeds alienation and resentment,” while NC spokesman Imran Nabi Dar suggested that entire villages were put under prolonged restrictions for days. The Omar Abdullah government , because of limited powers and no jurisdiction over the police in J&K, a Union Territory since 2019, finds itself hamstrung. The iron hand policy to stamp out terrorism and separatism has been effective from a strictly security perspective — terror attacks as well as local recruitments into terror ranks have declined. According to the police, local recruits have come down to single digit or fewer than 10 in Kashmir.

That said, the decline in terrorist incidents and the silence of the streets should not be mistaken for peace. The current situation demands a political reach-out by the Centre to all the stakeholders of J&K. It has to begin with the much-promised restoration of Statehood , which will give the voters a sense that their mass participation in the 2024 Assembly elections allowed their elected leaders to hold institutions accountable, and they were able to work freely to protect the interests of the region. Though the security agencies need to be focused on Pakistan-backed terrorism, it should not come at the cost of re-inflicting psychological scars within Kashmir, which could turn into a powder keg if left unattended. Healing through both political and security processes has to be complementary rather than conflicting. Allowing the political class of J&K to establish its writ and providing room to security agencies to combat challenges are not contradictory.
Editorial Context: Elusive peace: On Kashmir terror attack. This editorial examines the institutional, constitutional, and pragmatic dimensions shaping public policy and governance in India.

articles.title: All-too fallible: On India’s vote against moratorium on death penalty
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Death penalty requires a near-infallible criminal justice system

India’s vote against a proposed global moratorium on the death penalty at the UN is consistent with its position at the forum; it has defended its retention of the penalty as a sovereign decision backed by judicial safeguards, including the “rarest of rare” condition and sessions courts’ sentences requiring a High Court’s confirmation. At the same time, the Supreme Court has increasingly restricted capital punishment and research has failed to find evidence of additional deterrence over life imprisonment . India’s distinction between judicial executions and extrajudicial killings is legally valid but its further claim that due process protects people facing execution is less so. While India last executed convicts in 2020, for the Delhi gang-rape and murder, Parliament expanded the number of capital offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita — a form of penal populism that projects the political attractiveness of the state’s response to public outrage, especially in cases of sexual violence, without addressing the poor policing and low conviction rates that actually undermine deterrence . The country had 574 people on death row on December 31, 2025, the highest since 2016, thanks to trial court rulings, challenging claims about judicial safeguards in practice. The report of the 2015 Law Commission headed by Justice A.P. Shah said the death penalty “fails to achieve any constitutionally valid penological goals” and recommended abolishing it for all crimes except terrorism and waging war.

Only a small group of countries worldwide are executing more people. In India, per Project 39A, the Supreme Court released 38 persons from death row in 2016-2025 after they had spent eight years there on average. Some have endured more than two decades. The punishment requires a measure of infallibility that the criminal justice system cannot supply. The safeguards neither deter convictions in cases with flawed evidence, false testimony, and so on nor remedy unequal access to competent legal representation among those facing the penalty. India should formally suspend executions and commission a review of penalty statutes and the treatment of prisoners on death row. Second, it should spare offences that do not involve intentional killing from the penalty. Research suggests meting out excessively harsh punishments for non-fatal crimes could incentivise offenders to escalate their violence, including to kill potential witnesses. The greater goal should be to abolish the practice in law while improving investigative and prosecutorial practices and access to legal aid.

articles.title: Outlook outage: On Microsoft and dangers of centralising digital systems
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: The dangers of centralising the internet’s architecture are now clear

Last week, Microsoft’s suite of productivity and email software, which businesses, governments, hospitals and a host of other organisations rely upon round-the-clock, abruptly stopped working globally , affecting tens of millions of people around the world. The company has cited a network upgrade gone awry as the root cause of the incident. Incidents such as the Microsoft 365 outage are a natural consequence of businesses and governments allowing key digital systems to become centralised all over the world. The internet remains, and was pioneered as, a network of networks. If one business’s networks went down, the reasoning went, others would not fall like dominos: everyone was, after all, connected to everyone else. But the economics have long been prohibitive, with dedicated servers and web-connected infrastructure infeasible for all but the largest businesses, with even those firms seeking the enticing cost savings from socialised infrastructure. That made sense: the internet made shared infrastructure more economical, allowing hardware and maintenance costs to be spread so far and wide that at a per-user level prices have been negligible. Competition among major cloud providers, the few that remain at Microsoft’s scale, have kept prices affordable for enterprise software for all shades of organisations.

Digital services have grown more sophisticated, and more deeply integrated into the economy as this centralisation unfolded. But the downside is that, regardless of the sophistication and professionalism of any company, mistakes happen, and the scale of these mistakes can quickly cascade over to the entire economy. There are societal and organisational lessons to be gleaned from these episodes. There is no such thing as a reliable vendor. Governments must also draw a cyber sovereignty lesson here that does not simply entail swapping a global vendor for a domestic one. It is the subversion of the internet’s architecture that is at the root of these incidents. Investing in resilience — and shielding critical operations from destabilising disruptions, no matter how improbable — should inform attitudes to digital systems. As a new generation of AI data centres is poised to supercharge the centralised systems of yesteryear, it is all the more imperative to mitigate even occasional vagaries of large systems.

articles.title: Two months after deciding to drag the Centre to court, Maharashtra government decides to withdraw petition
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: FDA Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe had challenged FSSAI over the constitutional validity of a few regulations. The petition had challenged the creation of a few posts by the Centre, claiming it was against the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006

Two months after deciding to drag the Centre to court over a jurisdiction dispute, the Maharashtra government has taken a call to withdraw its petition, which had accused the Central government of usurping its power and creating new rules in a ‘clandestine manner’.

On September 3, 2026, Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration had filed a petition against FSSAI, challenging the constitutional validity of a few regulations. It had claimed that these regulations had led to the creation of ‘a parallel structure’ which ‘encroached upon the powers and duties of the State Commissioner of Food Safety and his officers.’ On October 29, the government directed officials to withdraw this petition, which had caused a stir as it led to a tussle between the Centre and the State, both governed by the Bharatiya Janata Party.

Political & National Report: Two months after deciding to drag the Centre to court, Maharashtra government decides to withdraw petition. This development is a key milestone in India's ongoing legislative, judicial, and constitutional governance framework.

articles.title: Emerging radicalisation hotspots now under purview of Multi-Agency Centre: Amit Shah
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Union Home Minister calls on anti-terrorism squads of every State to strengthen their cyber-expert units

The Multi-Agency Centre (MAC), a centralised intelligence-sharing platform, now tracks cybersecurity, narcotics, organised crime networks, and emerging radicalisation hotspots, Union Home Minister Amit Shah said on Thursday (November 19, 2026).

The MAC, which also acts as a common counter-terrorism grid and functions under the Intelligence Bureau (IB), was conceptualised in 2001, in the aftermath of the Kargil war, but became fully operational in 2009.
In 2025, the MAC network was revamped to connect all police districts in the country through a secure network. Mr. Shah said that the functioning of the MAC has been reorganised.
He said that the anti-terrorism squads (ATS) of every State needed to strengthen their cyber-expert units as technology is increasingly being used in such crimes.

He made the remarks while addressing the inaugural session of the two-day counter-terrorism conference organised by the National Investigation Agency (NIA) in New Delhi. On the occasion, he released the publication, Fail-Safe Investigation, brought out by the NIA. He also laid the foundation stone for the NIA’s office complex in Chandigarh and inaugurated the NIA’s residential complex at Maidangarhi in Delhi. In addition, the Union Home Minister e-launched the NIA’s ‘Pushti’ portal and conferred decorations on seven officers and personnel of the agency.

Union Home Secretary Govind Mohan, Intelligence Bureau Director Mahesh Dixit, Special Secretary (Internal Security) in the Ministry of Home Affairs, Anand Swarup, and NIA Director General Rakesh Aggarwal were present at the event.

Mr. Shah said that India has been confronting terrorism for a long time, and noted that while the police forces of different States had made various kinds of efforts, a lack of coordinated action was clearly visible. Over time, during the tenures of successive governments, gradual efforts were made to overcome these shortcomings, he said.

“Today, we can say with satisfaction that in this vast country — from Kashmir to Kanyakumari and from Dwarka to Kamakhya — we are putting in place a system under which a uniform strategy to combat terrorism will operate right down to the level of every police station,” the Home Minister said.

He said that with the killing of Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) terrorist Latif Bhat, Kashmir has become free from the presence of India-born terrorists, adding that this situation has come about after 35 years. He also said that more than 40 modules of the Shahzad Bhatti network, which has been declared a terrorist organisation under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), have been neutralised across the country.

Mr. Shah said that the hallmark of a successful agency is apprehending terrorists and putting them behind bars before they can carry out their plans. He said the police in every State should analyse this model and implement it in their respective areas.

articles.title: Women in high public office doesn’t mean equality throughout society: Justice Nagarathna
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Supreme Court judge says a woman may hold a senior position while other women remain excluded from education, employment, property, or effective legal remedies

Justice B.V. Nagarathna, one of the senior most judges of the Supreme Court and in line to be the first woman Chief Justice of India, has said that the mere existence of women in high public office does not establish that equality has been achieved throughout society.

“A woman may hold a senior position while other women remain excluded from education, employment, property, or effective legal remedies,” Justice Nagarathna said at the inaugural Cornelia Sorabji Memorial Lecture at Somerville College in the University of Oxford on Wednesday (November 18, 2026).
Only the practice of substantive equality could take care of these differences among women hailing from and living through diverse life experiences, the judge said.

Justice Nagarathna said a judgment cannot, by itself, guarantee that every workplace becomes safe, every girl receives education, every woman obtains her lawful inheritance, or every victim of domestic violence secures timely protection.
Likewise, legislation cannot achieve its full purpose if remedies were inaccessible, public authorities failed to act, or social attitudes prevent women from asserting their rights.

The judge said the enactment of Constitutional amendments which give women one-third of the seats in Parliament and the State legislatures was proof to show that women should participate in decision-making and not be content with just a formal right to vote.

“These developments reflect an important insight: where historical exclusion has shaped the composition of institutions, formal equality alone may not be sufficient to secure meaningful representation,” Justice Nagarathna pointed out.
Justice Nagarathna said that the progress of Indian women’s rights cannot be measured by the number of discriminatory provisions struck down or the enactment of a few beneficial laws.

The judge said recognition of violence against women as a violation of constitutional rights has not really translated in the real world to women seeking the protection of law without fear of stigma, retaliation or economic insecurity.

On the question of equality, Justice Nagarathna raised the fundamental problem of women being made to bear the “disproportionate burden of unpaid domestic and care work which continues to determine women’s choices”.

articles.title: Cyclone Akvan: Landfall process begins
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Director of Bhubaneswar Meteorological Centre Manorama Mohanty said the duration of the landfall process would be a long process which could stretch over seven to eight hours

The land interaction commenced as the sheared cloud mass associated with the cyclonic storm ‘Akvan’ entered into the north Andhra Pradesh-south Odisha coasts early on Friday, says the India Meteorological Department (IMD).

“Latest satellite imagery indicates the land interaction commenced as the sheared cloud mass associated with the Cyclonic Storm ‘Akvan’ entered into the north Andhra Pradesh-south Odisha coasts,” informed IMD on Friday (November 20, 2026).

The Severe Cyclonic Storm "Akvan" [Pronunciation: Akvan] over the westcentral Bay of Bengal moved north-northwestwards with the speed of 21 kmph during past 06 hours, weakened into a Cyclonic Storm and lay centered at 0230 hours IST of today, the 20th November, 2026 over the same region, near Latitude 17.7°N and Longitude 84.9°E, about 110 km southeast of Kalingapatnam (Andhra Pradesh), 170 km east of Visakhapatnam (Andhra Pradesh), 170 km south of Gopalpur (Odisha), 250 km south-southwest of Puri (Odisha) and 370 km east-northeast of Narsapur (Andhra Pradesh). It is likely to continue to move north-northwestward and cross North Andhra Pradesh and South Odisha coasts close to Gopalpur, by forenoon of 20th November, 2026 with the maximum sustained wind speed of 70-80 kmph gusting to 90 kmph. Latest Satellite imagery indicates the Land interaction commenced as the sheared cloud mass associated with the Cyclonic Storm "Akvan" entered into north Andhra Pradesh-south Odisha coasts. The system is under continuous surveillance of the Doppler Weather Radar at Visakhapatnam and Gopalpur.

“The severe cyclonic storm Akvan over the westcentral Bay of Bengal moved north-northwestwards with the speed of 21 kmph during the past six hours, weakened into a cyclonic storm and lay centred over the same region about 110 km southeast of Visakhapatnam (Andhra Pradesh) and 170 km south of Gopalpur (Odisha) and 250 km south-southwest of Puri (Odisha),” informed the IMD bulletin.

“It is likely to continue to move north-northwestward and cross the North Andhra Pradesh and South Odisha coasts close to Gopalpur by the forenoon of November 20, 2026, with the maximum sustained wind speed of 70-80 kmph, gusting to 90 kmph,” it further said.

Director of Bhubaneswar Meteorological Centre Manorama Mohanty said the duration of the landfall process would be a long process which could stretch over seven to eight hours. Meanwhile, coastal Odisha districts have started receiving heavy rain under the influence of the cyclone.

articles.title: Removal proceedings against me infructuous after resignation: Justice Varma tells Lok Sabha Secretariat
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: In a letter circulated among MPs on November 19, Justice Varma stated that the proceedings directed toward his removal did not survive his resignation

Justice Yashwant Varma has contended that proceedings for his removal as a High Court judge became infructuous following his resignation and cannot be continued, saying any attempt to remove him from office would be without constitutional foundation.
In a letter dated September 10 to Lok Sabha Secretary General Utpal Kumar Singh, he responded to the report of the inquiry committee constituted by Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla.
Mr. Varma wrote that the proceedings directed towards his removal did not survive his resignation.

He reiterated that he was innocent of the allegations against him, including the suggestion that he possessed ill-gotten funds, and asserted that his resignation should not be construed as an acknowledgement or admission of any allegation or finding.
The letter was circulated among MPs on Thursday (November 19, 2026).
The three-member inquiry committee, in its report tabled in Parliament on August 12, had found all three charges against Justice Varma proved .

The charges related to his failure to explain the presence, source or ownership of cash found at his official residence, failure to secure and preserve material evidence leading to the unexplained disappearance of the currency, and evasive and unsatisfactory explanations during the inquiry.

In a letter circulated among MPs on November 19, Justice Varma stated that the proceedings directed toward his removal did not survive his resignation

Justice Yashwant Varma has contended that proceedings for his removal as a High Court judge became infructuous following his resignation and cannot be continued, saying any attempt to remove him from office would be without constitutional foundation.

In a letter dated September 10 to Lok Sabha Secretary General Utpal Kumar Singh, he responded to the report of the inquiry committee constituted by Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla.

Mr. Varma wrote that the proceedings directed towards his removal did not survive his resignation.

He reiterated that he was innocent of the allegations against him, including the suggestion that he possessed ill-gotten funds, and asserted that his resignation should not be construed as an acknowledgement or admission of any allegation or finding.

The letter was circulated among MPs on Thursday (November 19, 2026).

The three-member inquiry committee, in its report tabled in Parliament on August 12, had found all three charges against Justice Varma proved .

The charges related to his failure to explain the presence, source or ownership of cash found at his official residence, failure to secure and preserve material evidence leading to the unexplained disappearance of the currency, and evasive and unsatisfactory explanations during the inquiry.

articles.title: Mahua Moitra alleges attack on her convoy by BJP supporters
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: BJP leaders said the alleged attack was Ms. Moitra’s attempt to gain attention and conduct self-promotion through social media live videos

Mamata All India Trinamool Congress lawmaker Mahua Moitra on Thursday (November 19, 2026) alleged that Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) members attacked her convoy when she was visiting her constituency — Krishnanagar — in Nadia district. She also accused the West Bengal police of inaction.

It is not the first time that the MP has been attacked since the BJP came to power in the State. “I have been attacked by the mob, with police waiting. My car was physically lifted. I have seen the same BJP member [I recognise his face] with flags,” Ms. Moitra said in a video statement after her car was attacked and vandalised.
She asked the Supreme Court, the Calcutta High Court, and the police to take note of the incident.

The Mamata loyalist also shared videos of BJP flags being carried by the mob that allegedly attacked her car and threw eggs at the windscreen. Ms. Moitra alleged that instead of rescuing her and neutralising the mob, the police personnel tried to stop her from attending her scheduled event in the area.
Meanwhile, Mamata's Trinamool general secretary Abhishek Banerjee and a Lok Sabha MP raised questions about the attack.

“Will the Calcutta High Court initiate contempt proceedings against the State Government and the Home Department for defying its orders, or does contempt of court apply only to the Opposition while those in power and their BJP allies enjoy special immunity?” Mr Banerjee asked.
West Bengal Industries Minister Tapas Roy said that without such incidents, Ms. Moitra does not get a chance to “go Live on Facebook”.

“She (Mahua Moitra) wants self-promotion. Now she does not have any other way of promotion, so these incidents are the only way for her to get some attention. If she wants, she can inform the court about any such incident,” Mr. Roy said.
On September 16, Ms. Moitra alleged that BJP workers pelted eggs on her during a visit to her Krishnanagar constituency in West Bengal’s Nadia.

articles.title: OPEC share in India’s crude imports drops to 27.4% in Apr-Oct amid West Asia flare-ups
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: During the mentioned period, India’s crude oil imports spurred about 2.7% to 146.6 million metric tonnes (MMT)

The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries’ (OPEC) share in India’s crude oil basket declined sharply to 27.4% during April-October of the current fiscal, against 38.5% in the corresponding period last year, according to the latest provisional data released by the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC).

The decline potentially reflects a shift in India’s crude procurement strategy as the country navigates shipping disruptions and geopolitical uncertainties arising from the continuing conflict in West Asia.
During the seven-month period, India’s crude oil imports increased 2.7% to 146.6 million metric tonnes (MMT).
Without identifying individual countries, PPAC data showed that supplies from the Eurasian region accounted for 43.8% of India’s crude oil import basket, while the Middle East contributed 36%.
South America accounted for 10.6% of imports, followed by Africa at 6.6% and North America at 3%.
The changing sourcing pattern indicates a growing diversification of India’s crude oil procurement, with supplies from outside the traditional Middle Eastern market gaining a larger share.

On the petroleum products trade front, diesel accounted for the largest share of India’s exports at 43.4% during the reported period. Petrol and aviation turbine fuel (ATF) followed with shares of 22.4% and 10%, respectively.
On the import side, liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) constituted the largest component, accounting for 50.5% of total petroleum product imports, followed by petroleum coke (petcoke) at 18.3%.
Petroleum product exports remain an important component of India’s external energy trade to contain the impact on its net oil and gas import bill.
Further, PPAC data released on Wednesday showed that petroleum product export volumes declined 13.5% year-on-year during April-October, even as their export value increased approximately 47%.

articles.title: How AI could reshape global growth and productivity
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: A key expected impact of AI is an unprecedented rise in labour productivity, as its success as a technological revolution is premised on such an increase; what remains to be seen is how pervasive its impact will be across different sectors of the economy

Many have likened the artificial intelligence (AI) phenomenon to the inventions of the steam engine or internal combustion engine in the 18th and 19th centuries, respectively. Only time can tell whether AI is epochal of that kind. In this two-part piece, we discuss the possible impact it may have on the global economy as a whole.

A key impact of AI is considered to be an unprecedented rise in labour productivity. In fact, if there is one purpose AI is supposed to serve, it is enhancing labour productivity multifold. Since labour productivity is a key variable in this puzzle, consider what it constitutes of (Box 1) . It is a ratio of output and workers employed. Now this ratio can rise in three different ways — a rise in output for a given number of workers employed (rise in the numerator); a loss of jobs which leads to a fall in the denominator; more jobs are created, but the output rises faster than the jobs (while both the numerator and the denominator are rising, the numerator rises faster than the denominator).

articles.title: India’s Oct. crude import bill soars 87.5% to $19.5-bn amid West Asia tensions, volumes up 11%
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: While higher petroleum product exports offer a partial natural hedge, sustained increases in crude and gas prices could intensify pressure on the country’s import bill.

India’s crude oil import bill surged 87.5% year-on-year (YoY) to $19.5 billion in October, as elevated international benchmark prices, fuelled by renewed tensions in West Asia, sharply increased procurement costs. The increase came alongside an 11% rise in import volumes.

The net import bill, calculated as imports of crude oil, petroleum products and natural gas less exports of petroleum products, rose 60% to $16 billion during the month, compared with $10 billion in October last year.
Higher export realisations from petroleum products, however, provided some cushion against the escalating import burden.

According to provisional data released by the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC), India imported 23.3 million metric tonnes (MMT) of crude oil in October, against 21 MMT in the corresponding month last year.
The expenditure on crude imports, meanwhile, climbed to $19.5 billion from $10.4 billion, reflecting the disproportionate impact of higher international prices on the country’s energy import bill.

The Indian crude oil basket averaged $119.91 per barrel in October, compared with $124.77 per barrel for Brent crude. In September, the Indian basket had averaged $116.09 per barrel, while Brent stood at $116.77 per barrel.

The sustained increase in benchmark prices, amid continuing geopolitical uncertainties in West Asia, has left India exposed to higher energy procurement costs, given its dependence on imported crude oil.
The impact of the rising crude import bill was partly offset by stronger earnings from petroleum product exports.
India’s petroleum product exports increased 5.9% in volume terms to 5.4 MMT in October. However, export revenues surged approximately 91% to $6.3 billion.
The increase in export earnings provided an important buffer against the higher cost of crude procurement.

While higher petroleum product exports offer a partial natural hedge, sustained increases in crude and gas prices could intensify pressure on the country’s import bill.

India’s crude oil import bill surged 87.5% year-on-year (YoY) to $19.5 billion in October, as elevated international benchmark prices, fuelled by renewed tensions in West Asia, sharply increased procurement costs. The increase came alongside an 11% rise in import volumes.

The net import bill, calculated as imports of crude oil, petroleum products and natural gas less exports of petroleum products, rose 60% to $16 billion during the month, compared with $10 billion in October last year.

Higher export realisations from petroleum products, however, provided some cushion against the escalating import burden.

According to provisional data released by the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC), India imported 23.3 million metric tonnes (MMT) of crude oil in October, against 21 MMT in the corresponding month last year.

The expenditure on crude imports, meanwhile, climbed to $19.5 billion from $10.4 billion, reflecting the disproportionate impact of higher international prices on the country’s energy import bill.

The Indian crude oil basket averaged $119.91 per barrel in October, compared with $124.77 per barrel for Brent crude. In September, the Indian basket had averaged $116.09 per barrel, while Brent stood at $116.77 per barrel.

The sustained increase in benchmark prices, amid continuing geopolitical uncertainties in West Asia, has left India exposed to higher energy procurement costs, given its dependence on imported crude oil.

The impact of the rising crude import bill was partly offset by stronger earnings from petroleum product exports.

India’s petroleum product exports increased 5.9% in volume terms to 5.4 MMT in October. However, export revenues surged approximately 91% to $6.3 billion.

The increase in export earnings provided an important buffer against the higher cost of crude procurement.

articles.title: India-U.S. trade deal signing will still ‘take some time’, says Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: He added that the deal can be signed only after the U.S. finalises its new tariff framework. Recently, Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said the two nations had agreed that India would receive an advantage over its competitors

The actual signing of the India-U.S. trade will still “take some time”, Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said on Wednesday (November 18, 2026), adding that the negotiation part and the legal text will be completed soon.

The delay in signing, he said, was because it can be done only after the U.S. concludes its Section 301 investigations into its trade partners and finalises its tariff structure. A few days ago, Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal asserted that the U.S. has acknowledged that India will receive lower tariffs as compared to its competitors.

“This is a deal that has been announced in February, the contours have already been announced as part of the joint statement,” Mr. Agrawal said while speaking at the curtain raiser of the FICCI Annual General Meeting. “The legal agreement has also been negotiated and it is now in final stages and it will be concluded soon.”
He was referring to the joint statement between India and the U.S. in February that announced the framework of an interim deal on trade.

However, Mr. Agrawal explained that the “challenge” is that this framework was announced against the background of the executive tariffs system that the U.S. President Donald Trump had put in place. At the time, the tariff on India was 50%. Later in February, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the legal foundation of these tariffs.

“Now a new tariff architecture is being created by the U.S.,” Mr. Agrawal explained. “So until that tariff architecture comes back in place, the signing of a deal is something that I think will take some time. But concluding the negotiations and having everything ready will be something that we will strive to achieve as soon as possible.”
In particular, Mr. Agrawal spoke about the investigations undertaken by the American administration under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.

One of these investigations, regarding forced labour, has been completed and a tariff of 10% has been levied on imports from India. The second investigation, looking into excess capacity, is yet to be completed and could come with further tariffs.

“There are certain 301 investigations which are already under review,” Mr. Agrawal said. “Those will also be coming to the fore in the next few weeks or months. You can’t have a deal until you have got uncertainty around multiple investigations which are already there.”

Separately, without mentioning the U.S. or any other country, Mr. Agrawal also asserted that trade deals can take a long time to conclude when parties try to maximise the benefits accruing to them rather than engaging in a spirit of compromise.

Even so, Ellerbroek’s enthusiasm for ‌the AI trade has waned.

“My beliefs about the growth in data centre capex spending have come down a little bit over the last month or two,” he added. “Nvidia’s crisis situation is a big deal. The midterm elections have had an impact. Data centres are ‌going to be more expensive to build and they’re going to be built more ​slowly.”
Advanced Micro Devices shares tumbled after investigative outlet Hunterbrook said its affiliated fund, Hunterbrook Capital, had taken a short position in the company.
Most chipmakers were ⁠lower, including Micron and Broadcom, among others.

articles.title: The Rohingya question: International solidarity, accountability and the missing road home
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The fundamental question remains: how does a community that has been systematically marginalised, displaced and denied its identity reclaim its place in the country it considers home?

The Rohingya question has returned to the centre of international attention following the landmark judgment delivered by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) on November 19, 2026. Yet, for more than a million Rohingya living outside Myanmar, legal recognition is only one part of a much larger struggle. The fundamental question remains: how does a community that has been systematically marginalised, displaced and denied its identity reclaim its place in the country it considers home? The crisis also exposes the international community’s inability to translate diplomatic declarations, humanitarian assistance and legal proceedings into a sustainable political settlement.

When I began working on Myanmar in the United Nations Department of Political Affairs in 2011, the Rohingya question was largely confined to perfunctory diplomatic talking points. Although concerns about discrimination, communal tensions and citizenship were acknowledged, there appeared to be limited understanding in many diplomatic discussions of the geographical and postcolonial nuances underlying the crisis.

This began to change with the outbreak of communal violence in May 2012, which dealt an early blow to Myanmar’s fragile democratisation process. The developments gradually compelled interlocutors to recognise that the country’s transition was not simply about moving away from military rule or introducing electoral reforms. It also involved confronting deeply entrenched postcolonial challenges, competing historical narratives, unresolved questions of identity and citizenship, and the complex relationship between the centre and its ethnic peripheries.

The Rohingya question could not be understood simply as another episode of communal tension between religious communities. It was deeply embedded in the history of colonial-era migration, the changing political geography of the Arakan region, competing narratives of belonging and the post-independence construction of citizenship in Myanmar. The historical relationship between the territories that now constitute Bangladesh and Myanmar, population movements during British colonial rule and the subsequent politicisation of identity were essential to understanding the dispute. The tendency to reduce the issue to a humanitarian concern or communal violence obscured these deeper historical and political dimensions.

The Rohingya question has returned to the centre of international attention following the landmark judgment delivered by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) on November 19, 2026. Yet, for more than a million Rohingya living outside Myanmar, legal recognition is only one part of a much larger struggle. The fundamental question remains: how does a community that has been systematically marginalised, displaced and denied its identity reclaim its place in the country it considers home? The crisis also exposes the international community’s inability to translate diplomatic declarations, humanitarian assistance and legal proceedings into a sustainable political settlement.

When I began working on Myanmar in the United Nations Department of Political Affairs in 2011, the Rohingya question was largely confined to perfunctory diplomatic talking points. Although concerns about discrimination, communal tensions and citizenship were acknowledged, there appeared to be limited understanding in many diplomatic discussions of the geographical and postcolonial nuances underlying the crisis.

This began to change with the outbreak of communal violence in May 2012, which dealt an early blow to Myanmar’s fragile democratisation process. The developments gradually compelled interlocutors to recognise that the country’s transition was not simply about moving away from military rule or introducing electoral reforms. It also involved confronting deeply entrenched postcolonial challenges, competing historical narratives, unresolved questions of identity and citizenship, and the complex relationship between the centre and its ethnic peripheries.

The Rohingya question could not be understood simply as another episode of communal tension between religious communities. It was deeply embedded in the history of colonial-era migration, the changing political geography of the Arakan region, competing narratives of belonging and the post-independence construction of citizenship in Myanmar. The historical relationship between the territories that now constitute Bangladesh and Myanmar, population movements during British colonial rule and the subsequent politicisation of identity were essential to understanding the dispute. The tendency to reduce the issue to a humanitarian concern or communal violence obscured these deeper historical and political dimensions.

articles.title: Draft of COP31 cover text drops references to fossil fuel phase-out, net zero dates
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: A major concern raised by developing countries, of phasing out unilateral trade measures such as the CBAM (Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism) by 2027, that was present in the earlier draft has also been eliminated

The latest iteration of the COP 31 draft cover text has eliminated references to fossil fuel phase-out and net-zero dates but has also deleted references to a firm $120 billion adaptation-finance target that developing countries have been asking for as “legally binding financial obligations” on developed countries. This suggests that the most ambitious demands of both the developed and developing country blocs have been eliminated.

A cover text is an overarching political decision that frames the outcome of a climate conference rather than settling any single agenda item. It is usually finalised last, and like every outcome it needs the consensus of all Parties. The Presidency has said earlier drafts were not meant to reflect consensus.

The COP31 Presidency’s revised draft cover decision, dated November 19, has 80 paragraphs, down from 144 in the November 16 version. The summit officially ends on November 20, though negotiations frequently overshoot into the weekend.

A major concern raised by developing countries, of phasing out unilateral trade measures such as the CBAM (Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism) by 2027, that was present in the earlier draft has also been eliminated.

However, a widely expected outcome of raising electricity’s share in final energy consumption to 35% by 2035, scaling up the use of carbon capture utilisation technologies and making early warning systems universal by 2027, continue to find mention in the text. A broad commitment to triple adaptation finance also remains.

“ The draft cover text weaves the 35% electricity in final energy consumption by 2035, alongside tripling renewable energy capacity and doubling the rate of energy efficiency improvement by 2030, ” Ajay Mathur, India’s lead negotiator at Paris COP and former DG, International Solar Alliance, said in a statement. The electricity use in India went up by 13% in 2025 due to the Hormuz crisis alone. It will be an ambitious goal for India to achieve 35% electrification by 2035, but due to the increasing amount of renewable energy in the Indian energy mix, we will be near the 32-34% mark by 2035. ”

“We’re down to the wire at COP31, and the latest texts are alarmingly far from ambitious or equitable,” said Rachel Cleetus, Climate Program director at the Union of Concerned Scientists (UCS) in a statement. “Rich nations, most notably the EU nations, are still holding a harsh line against committing to tripling adaptation finance to at least $120 billion annually by 2035. Instead of reaching agreement on urgently needed climate finance, some countries seem willing to push negotiations toward failure.”

articles.title: Israel army says it completed ground operation in central Gaza
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Hamas denounced a "blatant ceasefire violation," while the military said the rare ground incursion was a response to Hamas ceasefire violations in the area
Israel's military said that a ground operation involving tanks in central Gaza that began the previous day despite a U.S.-brokered ceasefire had come to an end on Thursday (November 19, 2026).

The Defence Ministry's body in charge of civilian affairs in Palestinian territories, Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT), said in a statement that Palestinians would again be free to move in the targeted areas near the Al-Bureij and Nuseirat refugee camps.

"We would like to inform you that the activity has ended, and the Salah al-Din axis has been reopened," COGAT said in an Arabic-language statement on Facebook, referring to the war-shattered territory's main thoroughfare.

On Wednesday (November 18, 2026), the Israeli military said it had launched an operation in a Hamas-controlled area of central Gaza, beyond the so-called "Yellow Line" which separates areas under Israeli military and Hamas control following an October 2025 ceasefire.
An AFP journalist reported seeing Israeli tanks positioning themselves east of the Nuseirat refugee camp.
Hamas denounced a "blatant ceasefire violation," while the military said the rare ground incursion was a response to Hamas ceasefire violations in the area.
The military said in a statement that the operation had been launched to "dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".

A Gaza security source told AFP there had been "intense Israeli artillery shelling" north of Nuseirat refugee camp and reported Israeli military vehicles in central Gaza "amid ongoing gunfire and airstrikes since midday".
Israel and Hamas regularly accuse each other of violating the U.S.-brokered ceasefire deal that came after two years of devastating war sparked by Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack on Israel.

More than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the ceasefire, according to an AFP tally based on data from the Gaza Health Ministry, which operates under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.

articles.title: Third Ukrainian strike in 4 days halts rail traffic on Russia's Kerch Bridge to Crimea
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The attack came hours before the start of talks in Berlin between U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy alongside more than 40 European leaders who are supporting Ukraine's war effort

A third Ukrainian aerial attack in four days on the key Kerch Bridge linking Russia to Russian-held Crimea halted rail traffic across the span, officials said Thursday (November 19, 2026), after earlier strikes shut down the road section of the landmark that is a symbol of Moscow's invasion.
Train traffic across the bridge stopped after the overnight strike while authorities assessed the damage, but it resumed in the afternoon, according to Russian state news agency RIA Novosti .

The Ukrainian strikes seemed calculated to embarrass Russian President Vladimir Putin as he met in China with President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump, as well as to demonstrate that Kyiv still holds cards in the war and to undermine Russia's argument that its victory is inevitable.

The attack came hours before the start of talks in Berlin between U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy alongside more than 40 European leaders who are supporting Ukraine's war effort and fear being sidelined by Mr. Trump's direct talks with Mr. Putin.
“We will respond to these attacks, and I want everyone to be clear about that,” Mr. Putin told reporters in Shenzhen, China.
He insisted the bridge is a civilian asset, adding that he had ordered the bridge closed to the transport of military hardware or ammunition.
Mr. Putin also said that the road side of the bridge had been “seriously damaged” but vowed to rebuild it.
The rail section is believed to be stronger than the road side, to bear the greater weight of cargo wagons.

The 19-kilometre (12-mile) Kerch Bridge is a key route for military and civilian supplies to Crimea, which Moscow seized in defiance of international law in 2014 and uses to support front-line troops. It is a potent reminder of Russia's illegal annexation of the territory and has been a prime target for Ukraine.

A large section of the road deck and an arch collapsed in the culmination of weeks of preparatory strikes over seven stages of the operation, according to Mr. Zelenskyy, and the train track was damaged by domestically produced Neptune missiles, Ukraine's Defence Ministry said.

articles.title: Anthropic raises $81 billion in IPO amid AI market volatility
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The Claude maker priced its shares at $83 apiece, implying an equity valuation of about $1.03 trillion based on outstanding shares, with trading scheduled to begin on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on November 19

Anthropic, the maker of artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude, has priced its initial public offering (IPO) at $83 a share, valuing the offering at approximately $81.34 billion, according to an announcement by the company on November 18.

The company said its shares were expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on November 19 under the ticker symbol ANT. The offering is expected to close on November 20, subject to customary closing conditions.

According to Anthropic’s announcement, the offering comprises 980 million shares of Class A common stock. Of these, 956.35 million shares are being sold by the company and 23.65 million by existing shareholders. Anthropic said it would not receive any proceeds from the sale of shares by the selling shareholders.

At the IPO price of $83 a share, the company’s portion of the offering is valued at approximately $79.38 billion, while the shares sold by existing shareholders are valued at approximately $1.96 billion. These figures are before underwriting discounts and expenses.
At $83 a share, Anthropic’s overall equity value works out to approximately $1.03 trillion, based on the total number of shares outstanding after the IPO.
Anthropic has also given the banks (underwriters) managing the IPO the option to purchase an additional 147 million shares within 30 days, potentially increasing the size of the offering.
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the lead underwriters for the IPO, with JPMorgan, Citigroup, Barclays and other investment banks also participating, according to the SEC filing.
The IPO comes amid growing investor concerns over the sustainability of the AI investment boom and whether technology companies can generate sufficient returns from their infrastructure spending.
On November 5, the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5%, wiping out trillions of dollars in market value, while NVIDIA shares declined 9% and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped 12%.

Earlier, on October 29, Alphabet shares plunged 12.6%, wiping out approximately $500 billion in market value after its quarterly results raised concerns over its advertising business and the cash-flow impact of rising AI investments. The sell-off reflected broader concerns over the valuations of AI-linked companies and the returns from their heavy spending on data centres and computing infrastructure.

articles.title: Why data interoperability is critical to the future of hospital care
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The future of critical care will be defined by how effectively the information is connected, interpreted and applied

In an intensive care unit, every second matters. A critically ill patient may be connected to several devices, including patient monitors, ventilators and infusion pumps, while laboratory systems and electronic health records continuously generate additional information. Together, these systems create a large and rapidly-changing picture of the patient’s condition. However, when the information remains fragmented across devices and platforms, clinicians may spend valuable time locating, verifying and reconciling data before they can act.

This makes interoperability a clinical priority in critical care, not simply an information technology requirement. Integration enables systems to exchange data, but true interoperability ensures that the information being exchanged is accurate, interpretable and clinically relevant. This can help care teams coordinate and prioritise interventions more effectively while reducing the need to move between multiple systems to assemble a clinical picture.

The future of critical care will be defined by how effectively the information is connected, interpreted and applied

In an intensive care unit, every second matters. A critically ill patient may be connected to several devices, including patient monitors, ventilators and infusion pumps, while laboratory systems and electronic health records continuously generate additional information. Together, these systems create a large and rapidly-changing picture of the patient’s condition. However, when the information remains fragmented across devices and platforms, clinicians may spend valuable time locating, verifying and reconciling data before they can act.

This makes interoperability a clinical priority in critical care, not simply an information technology requirement. Integration enables systems to exchange data, but true interoperability ensures that the information being exchanged is accurate, interpretable and clinically relevant. This can help care teams coordinate and prioritise interventions more effectively while reducing the need to move between multiple systems to assemble a clinical picture.

articles.title: How U.S. controls flow of advanced tech, chip, and compute to China | Explained
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The U.S. Commerce Department, on November 16, 2026, issued an interim final rule barring data centre operators outside of the U.S., equipped with advanced American AI chips, from providing cloud service to businesses in two dozen countries, including China, Iran and Russia

The story so far: The battle for the most sought after commodity that underpins development of artificial intelligence technology just grew fiercer after the U.S. Commerce Department, on November 16, 2026, issued an interim final rule (IFR) barring data centre operators outside of the U.S., equipped with advanced American AI chips, from providing cloud service to businesses in two dozen countries, including China, Iran and Russia. The new, yet to be published, rule also restricts American companies from freely shipping high-end AI chips to a set of five countries, including Indonesia, Malaysia, and Singapore, without the explicit approval of the U.S. government.

China has censured the move, calling it “yet another case of the U.S. overstretching the concept of national security, and abusing export control measures to interfere in normal trade and tech cooperation between China and other countries and go after China’s high-tech industry.”
The interim rule came just days ahead of the meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China on the sidelines of the November 18-19 APEC Summit.

The U.S. government’s policy on making advanced technology inaccessible to China has been a talking point among lawmakers in Washington for well over a decade, but a legal tool to control the flow took shape only during the first Trump term when the administration passed the Export Control Reform Act in 2018.

It gave the U.S. a legal weapon to control the movement of advanced technology originating from the country. Its primary purpose was to curb export of top-tier chips that had dual-use — both commercial and military purposes — to countries like China, Russia and Iran.

articles.title: Hyderabad doctor brings down rare disease drug cost from ₹9 crore to ₹2.5 lakh; seven children to get free treatment
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Seven children diagnosed with Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome (AHDS), a rare genetic disorder, are set to receive a year’s supply of the medicine tiratricol free of cost on November 30; the compounded formulation is estimated to cost just ₹2.5 lakh per child for a year

Imagine having a medicine that could help manage your child’s rare genetic condition, but being unable to afford it because a year’s treatment costs as much as ₹9 crore. For seven families in India, that situation could soon change.

Seven children diagnosed with Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome (AHDS), a rare genetic disorder, are set to receive a year’s supply of the medicine tiratricol free of cost on November 30, following an initiative led by Hyderabad-based paediatrician Dr. Sivaranjani Santosh and Access to Medicines India.

The development is significant not just because the families will receive the medicine without paying for it, but also because its cost has been brought down through pharmaceutical compounding in the Netherlands. While the commercial version of the drug costs approximately ₹4.68 crore to ₹9 crore per child annually, the compounded formulation is estimated to cost just ₹2.5 lakh per child for a year.

The medicine has been prepared by Transvaal Pharmacy in The Hague, Netherlands, with support from the Netherlands-based Pharmaceutical Accountability Foundation (PAF). The first batch will be handed over to the parents of the seven children along with the necessary documentation and individual import permissions. The families have secured approvals for one year of treatment. As the compounded medicine has a shelf life of six months, it will be imported in two batches.

The initiative began after Arav, a child under the care of Dr. Sivaranjani, was diagnosed with AHDS, also known as MCT8 deficiency. The condition is caused by mutations affecting the MCT8 gene, which plays an important role in transporting thyroid hormones into brain cells. Tiratricol, also known as TRIAC, acts on thyroid hormone receptors and may help overcome some effects of the deficiency. It also helps minimise complications associated with peripheral thyrotoxicosis.

Although the medicine was available in Europe, its commercial price put it beyond the reach of most Indian families. Arav’s mother, Pavitra Sirolkar, had to arrange approximately ₹12 lakh to ₹13 lakh for just one month’s supply of the medicine from Germany. Dr. Sivaranjani initially approached paediatricians, endocrinologists and paediatric neurologists to explore ways of procuring the drug. Doctors at Christian Medical College (CMC), Vellore, where five other children with the same condition had been identified, were also approached.

Attempts to obtain the medicine through pharmaceutical company Egetis Therapeutics and its compassionate-use programme did not succeed. The situation eventually prompted Dr. Sivaranjani to take the issue to social media. On September 7, she posted an appeal seeking help for the family and urged people to tag the Prime Minister, Union Health Minister and other government representatives. The appeal gained attention, bringing it to the notice of PAF.

The foundation subsequently explored the possibility of preparing the medicine through pharmaceutical compounding using the active pharmaceutical ingredient. Transvaal Pharmacy conducted test batches and developed a formulation for the seven children. The initial group included Arav and five children receiving treatment at CMC Vellore. A seventh child, aged one year, was identified after his father contacted Dr Sivaranjani following her social media appeal.

According to PAF, the total cost of providing one year’s treatment to all seven children is €14,200, approximately ₹15.08 lakh. Of this, Dr Sivaranjani raised approximately ₹6.09 lakh in India, while PAF undertook to raise the remaining €8,600, approximately ₹9.13 lakh, in the Netherlands. The medicine will be provided to all seven families free of cost.

While the November 30 handover addresses the immediate treatment requirements of the seven children, Dr. Sivaranjani believes that importing the medicine cannot be a permanent solution. She plans to approach the Union government and work with Access to Medicines India and other organisations to explore the possibility of getting the medicine compounded in India and making it accessible to more children.

📰 Hyderabad doctor brings down rare disease drug cost from ₹9 crore to ₹2.5 lakh; seven children to get free treatment

🎯 Exam Relevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action

Seven children diagnosed with Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome (AHDS), a rare genetic disorder, are set to receive a year’s supply of the medicine tiratricol free of cost on November 30; the compounded formulation is estimated to cost just ₹2.5 lakh per child for a year

Imagine having a medicine that could help manage your child’s rare genetic condition, but being unable to afford it because a year’s treatment costs as much as ₹9 crore. For seven families in India, that situation could soon change.

Seven children diagnosed with Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome (AHDS), a rare genetic disorder, are set to receive a year’s supply of the medicine tiratricol free of cost on November 30, following an initiative led by Hyderabad-based paediatrician Dr. Sivaranjani Santosh and Access to Medicines India.

The development is significant not just because the families will receive the medicine without paying for it, but also because its cost has been brought down through pharmaceutical compounding in the Netherlands. While the commercial version of the drug costs approximately ₹4.68 crore to ₹9 crore per child annually, the compounded formulation is estimated to cost just ₹2.5 lakh per child for a year.

The medicine has been prepared by Transvaal Pharmacy in The Hague, Netherlands, with support from the Netherlands-based Pharmaceutical Accountability Foundation (PAF). The first batch will be handed over to the parents of the seven children along with the necessary documentation and individual import permissions. The families have secured approvals for one year of treatment. As the compounded medicine has a shelf life of six months, it will be imported in two batches.

The initiative began after Arav, a child under the care of Dr. Sivaranjani, was diagnosed with AHDS, also known as MCT8 deficiency. The condition is caused by mutations affecting the MCT8 gene, which plays an important role in transporting thyroid hormones into brain cells. Tiratricol, also known as TRIAC, acts on thyroid hormone receptors and may help overcome some effects of the deficiency. It also helps minimise complications associated with peripheral thyrotoxicosis.

Although the medicine was available in Europe, its commercial price put it beyond the reach of most Indian families. Arav’s mother, Pavitra Sirolkar, had to arrange approximately ₹12 lakh to ₹13 lakh for just one month’s supply of the medicine from Germany. Dr. Sivaranjani initially approached paediatricians, endocrinologists and paediatric neurologists to explore ways of procuring the drug. Doctors at Christian Medical College (CMC), Vellore, where five other children with the same condition had been identified, were also approached.

Attempts to obtain the medicine through pharmaceutical company Egetis Therapeutics and its compassionate-use programme did not succeed. The situation eventually prompted Dr. Sivaranjani to take the issue to social media. On September 7, she posted an appeal seeking help for the family and urged people to tag the Prime Minister, Union Health Minister and other government representatives. The appeal gained attention, bringing it to the notice of PAF.

The foundation subsequently explored the possibility of preparing the medicine through pharmaceutical compounding using the active pharmaceutical ingredient. Transvaal Pharmacy conducted test batches and developed a formulation for the seven children. The initial group included Arav and five children receiving treatment at CMC Vellore. A seventh child, aged one year, was identified after his father contacted Dr Sivaranjani following her social media appeal.

According to PAF, the total cost of providing one year’s treatment to all seven children is €14,200, approximately ₹15.08 lakh. Of this, Dr Sivaranjani raised approximately ₹6.09 lakh in India, while PAF undertook to raise the remaining €8,600, approximately ₹9.13 lakh, in the Netherlands. The medicine will be provided to all seven families free of cost.

While the November 30 handover addresses the immediate treatment requirements of the seven children, Dr. Sivaranjani believes that importing the medicine cannot be a permanent solution. She plans to approach the Union government and work with Access to Medicines India and other organisations to explore the possibility of getting the medicine compounded in India and making it accessible to more children.

articles.title: GTA VI generates record $1.1 billion pre-order revenue
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: With record pre-orders and broad market reach, GTA VI is positioned to dominate digital engagement through the end of the year

As Grand Theft Auto (GTA) VI officially launches today , November 19, 2026, a market intelligence report from Sensor Tower highlights an unprecedented shift in consumer engagement and industry revenue.

According to Sensor Tower’s report, the title generated $1.1 billion in pre-order revenue globally across PlayStation and Xbox consoles prior to release, with 11.3 million copies sold. This accomplishment marks the largest pre-launch revenue total on record.

The analytics firms project that total sales could reach $3.2 billion by the end of 2026. Beyond financial performance, the report forecasts a noticeable reallocation of consumer attention across the broader digital landscape.
Daily active user metrics across competing games and entertainment platforms are expected to see a measurable decline as players engage with the new release.
Sensor Tower estimates the average GTA VI player age at approximately 34 years old. This audience displays high companion engagement on second-screen platforms, including Discord, TikTok, and Twitch.
With record pre-orders and broad market reach, GTA VI is positioned to dominate digital engagement through the end of the year.

Investing in resilience — and shielding critical operations from destabilising disruptions, no matter how improbable — should inform attitudes to digital systems.
